summary: Describes where the ForCES model and protocol apply. ForCES separates control elements from forwarding elements in routers and similar devices. The document gives example deployment scenarios and functionality. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Inside a router, one part decides and another part moves packets. This document shows where it makes sense to split those parts into separate boxes.

questions: when to use forwarding and control element separation
subtitle: Defining where the ForCES protocol for separating control and forwarding in routers is appropriate and useful.

tldr.problem: High-end routers often separate control-plane functions (routing, policy) from data-plane functions (packet forwarding), requiring a standard protocol for them to communicate.
tldr.mechanism: ForCES defines a protocol and model for this control-plane-to-data-plane communication, applicable when control and forwarding elements need to exchange capability information, configuration, routing tables, QoS settings, and status.
tldr.outcome: Router vendors and operators can build modular, scalable routers with independent control and forwarding blades that cooperate over a standard interface, rather than monolithic designs.

today: RFC 6041 is an Informational statement describing the applicability of ForCES. The ForCES protocol family (RFCs 5810-5813) is standardized, and ForCES remains applicable in high-end routers and network devices that require standard control-plane-to-data-plane communication.

sections.title: The ForCES Architecture
sections.content:
Modern high-end IP routers typically separate control-plane functions from data-plane (forwarding) functions. The control plane runs routing protocols, policy logic, and admission control. The data plane performs the fast, per-packet operations: forwarding decisions, queuing, and header editing. These two planes often run on separate hardware components and must communicate: the control element (CE) sends forwarding tables and policy to the forwarding elements (FEs), and the FEs report their capabilities and operational status to the CEs.

The ForCES protocol provides a standard framework and message format for this control-to-forwarding communication. It is designed for high-end routers and similar devices where this separation occurs and where a standard communication mechanism is valuable for interoperability.
sections.plainLanguage: A router has a brain (control) that decides and hands (forwarding) that move packets. ForCES is the language they use to talk to each other.

sections.title: When ForCES Applies
sections.content:
ForCES is most applicable to high-end routing systems that distribute control and forwarding work across multiple processing elements. ForCES is not useful for simple, low-end routing systems implemented on a single piece of hardware where control and forwarding run together.

ForCES assumes that control elements and forwarding elements have already discovered each other through static configuration or a separate discovery protocol. The ForCES protocol takes over after that point. It supports architectures with a primary control element and multiple secondary CEs for high availability, and it supports multiple forwarding elements in a single router.
sections.plainLanguage: It's useful only for big, complex routers. Simple routers don't need it because they do everything in one place.

sections.title: Services Supported by ForCES
sections.content:
ForCES enables control elements and forwarding elements to exchange a wide range of information. Association and capability discovery is the first phase: CEs and FEs describe their capabilities and attributes (number of ports, configurable parameters, supported features) to each other. Configuration allows CEs to set FE attributes like IP addresses and enabled features.

Routing exchange lets CEs send forwarding tables and routing updates to FEs. QoS exchange allows FEs to advertise queuing, metering, and policing capabilities, which the CE can then configure. Security exchange covers negotiation of encryption and tunnel configuration. ForCES also supports topology information exchange (once topology is determined by other means), filtering and firewall configuration, encapsulation and tunneling setup, NAT configuration, and measurement and accounting settings.

Additionally, ForCES enables diagnostics (FEs can report self-test results) and redundancy and failover through mechanisms that ensure atomicity across the network element when multiple CEs or FEs are present.
sections.plainLanguage: The control part can tell the forwarding part: here are my features, here are the settings, here's the routing table, here are the security rules, and so on.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios and Locality
sections.content:
ForCES operates in two locality models. In a single-box NE (network element), control and forwarding blades live in the same physical chassis and share a high-reliability interconnect such as Ethernet or PCI. The control traffic typically does not traverse the same links as forwarded data traffic. This is the primary use case and achieves both modularity and high reliability.

In a multiple-box NE, control and forwarding elements are physically separated, ranging from being in the same rack to being in different buildings or continents. ForCES is applicable as long as the reliability of the CE-FE control link does not significantly degrade the overall router reliability. For example, if the control link's failure would also disable the FE's primary forwarding connections, then the overall impact on reliability is acceptable. ForCES should not be deployed over control links that are significantly less reliable than the forwarding data paths.

The bandwidth of the CE-FE control link is a consideration: forwarding tables can grow to very large sizes, and they must be transmitted over this link. The protocol is designed to be future-proof as routing tables grow.
sections.plainLanguage: You can put the brain and hands in one box (best case) or split them across boxes that are far apart, as long as they can talk reliably.

sections.title: Management and Security
sections.content:
From a management perspective, a ForCES NE should appear as a single router to external management systems, even though internally it is composed of multiple control and forwarding elements. Management commands arrive at the CE, which then uses ForCES to instruct the FEs. A ForCES MIB (management information base) is defined for monitoring the ForCES protocol itself—it tracks association state, configuration parameters, and statistics between CEs and FEs.

ForCES includes optional security features such as mutual authentication of CEs and FEs, message integrity, and confidentiality, typically provided through IPsec or TLS. An operator may choose to use all, some, or none of these security services depending on the security requirements and the physical security of the CE-FE interconnect.

ForCES assumes that CEs and FEs have sufficient information to begin communication securely, such as pre-shared keys or certificates. The protocol does not specify how this initial trust is established.
sections.plainLanguage: From the outside, the split router looks like one router. Security features are optional depending on how much you trust your interconnect.
